newton-isaac.simple: English natural philosopher and mathematician (1643–1727) who also wrote a formal commentary on Daniel and Revelation, published in 1733 as Observations upon the Prophecies of Daniel, and the Apocalypse of St. John.
newton-isaac.history: Newton did not treat Daniel as a sealed riddle. In Part I, Chapter I he wrote that Daniel is “most distinct in order of time, and easiest to be understood,” and that for “things which relate to the last times, he must be made the key to the rest.” That is historicism in one sentence: a dated sequence of real kingdoms read in order. In Part I, Chapter III he reads Daniel 2’s metals as Babylonia, the Persians, the Greeks, and the Romans in historical succession; in Chapter VII, on the eleventh horn, he applies the horn to the Church of Rome and its Bishop. This course cites Newton as an eighteenth-century witness to the continuous chain, not as an infallible guide on every horn detail—test each claim against Scripture.
proof: Primary: Sir Isaac Newton, Observations upon the Prophecies of Daniel (London, 1733), Part I, Chap. I — “Daniel is most distinct in order of time, and easiest to be understood” (Gutenberg 16878).
Primary: Newton, Observations, Part I, Chap. III — “Of the vision of the Image composed of four Metals”: Babylonia, the Persians, the Greeks, and the Romans.
Primary: Newton, Observations, Part I, Chap. VII — “Of the eleventh horn of Daniel’s fourth Beast”: the Church of Rome and its Bishop.
Compare Newton’s “order of time” with the three-school table in Sitting 0 and ask which reading keeps that order.

hermeneutics.simple: The rules you use before you name a king, a horn, or a date — the method that decides whether Daniel is one timeline or a book that ends in the second century B.C. or jumps to a future seven-year crisis.
hermeneutics.history: Every sitting assumes a hermeneutical choice. Historicism reads Daniel and Revelation as one unbroken chain of real empires from the exile toward Christ’s return. Preterism (Alcázar, 1614) parks most of Daniel in the Maccabean era; futurism (Ribera, c. 1590) inserts a long gap before a future Antichrist week. Protestant futurism spread through S. R. Maitland (1826); Darby’s dispensationalism, popularized by the 1909 Scofield Reference Bible, made the gap familiar in English pews. The course defends historicism because Daniel’s succession language, parallel visions, and internal date tests (Daniel 9) fit a continuous historical reading when Scripture interprets Scripture.
proof: Scripture (KJV): Daniel 2:38–40; 7:3–7 — succession of kingdoms named or implied in order.
Witness: Hippolytus, Treatise on Christ and Antichrist §28 (c. A.D. 200) — gold, silver, brass, and iron as Babylon, Persia and Media, Greece, and Rome, one chain.
Witness: Luis de Alcázar, Vestigatio (1614) vs Francisco Ribera, Revelation commentary (c. 1590) — dated Counter-Reformation alternatives named in Sitting 0.

historicism.simple: Read Daniel and Revelation as one unbroken timeline of real empires from the prophet’s day through the Christian era to the stone kingdom and the Second Coming.
historicism.history: Historicism is the reading this course defends: Babylon → Medo-Persia → Greece → Rome → divided Europe → Christ’s kingdom, without parking the book in 164 B.C. or freezing it until a future seven-year crisis. Hippolytus (c. A.D. 200) already lists Babylon, Persia, Greece, and Rome as one sequence. Newton, in 1733, still called Daniel “most distinct in order of time” and read the four metals as Babylonia, the Persians, the Greeks, and the Romans. Preterism and futurism are the rejected alternatives, with dated authors Alcázar (1614) and Ribera (1590).
proof: Scripture (KJV): Daniel 2:44 — kingdom set up “in the days of these kings” (the divided feet), not during Babylon alone.
Witness: Hippolytus, Treatise on Christ and Antichrist §28 — the golden head through the iron legs as Babylon through Rome.
Primary: Newton 1733, Part I, Chap. I — Daniel “most distinct in order of time” (Gutenberg 16878).

preterism.simple: The claim that most of Daniel (and often Revelation) was already fulfilled in the distant past — especially under Antiochus IV in the 160s B.C. or at Jerusalem’s fall in A.D. 70.
preterism.history: Porphyry (3rd century) argued Daniel was written after Antiochus; Jerome reports and answers that charge. Jesuit Luis de Alcázar (1614, Vestigatio Arcani Sensus in Apocalypsi) systematized a preterist reading that leaves no medieval or modern church on the chain. That move serves Counter-Reformation polemics: if prophecy ended in antiquity, Rome cannot be on Daniel 7’s horn. This course rejects full preterism because Gabriel places Daniel 8 at “the time of the end” (8:17; cf. 8:19), which Antiochus cannot exhaust, and because Daniel 2:44 requires a kingdom after Rome’s division.
proof: Witness: Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, Prologue — the Porphyry late-date charge he answers.
Primary: Alcázar, Vestigatio arcani sensus in Apocalypsi (1614) — the preterist template (Sitting 0).
Scripture (KJV): Daniel 8:17; cf. 8:19 — the vision concerns “the time of the end,” not only 164 B.C.

futurism.simple: The claim that Daniel’s hardest numbers — especially the 70th week — jump to a future individual Antichrist after a long unstated gap in the text itself.
futurism.history: Patristic readers already expected a future antichrist (Hippolytus). Francisco Ribera’s c. 1590 Revelation commentary made the gap systematic: Antichrist as one man for 3½ literal years, severing the 70th week from the first 69. Protestant adoption followed through S. R. Maitland (1826), Edward Irving, John Nelson Darby, and the 1909 Scofield Reference Bible. Gabriel never writes a two-thousand-year parenthesis into Daniel 9. This sitting names Ribera and Darby so learners see a dated 19th-century shift, not an anonymous “always read it this way.”
proof: Primary: Francisco Ribera, Revelation commentary (c. 1590 / 1593 Lyon) — futurist gap-week template (Sitting 0).
Witness: S. R. Maitland (1826) — Protestant uptake (Sitting 0).
Scripture (KJV): Daniel 9:24–27 — seventy weeks as one decree-to-Messiah structure; gap is interpretive, not lexical.

year-day.simple: When God attaches a numbered sign to symbolic prophecy, one prophetic day may stand for one literal solar year — the scale Scripture states before Daniel applies it.
year-day.history: God fixes the rod twice: Numbers 14:34 (forty spy-days become forty wilderness years, “each day for a year”) and Ezekiel 4:6 (Ezekiel’s lying-days appointed the same way). Daniel 9 then uses seventy weeks — 490 units — to span decree, rebuilt city, and Messiah; 490 ordinary days cannot hold that narrative, so the book tests the scale on itself. On the course’s reading, the same rod measures 1,260 days (Daniel 7:25) and 2,300 evenings-mornings (Daniel 8:14). 2 Peter 3:8 says “one day is with the Lord as a thousand years,” in the context of the Lord’s patience (2 Peter 3:9), not as a day-for-year rule for numbered visions.
proof: Scripture (KJV): Numbers 14:34; Ezekiel 4:6 — explicit day-for-year appointments (Sitting 0).
Scripture (KJV): Daniel 9:24–25 — seventy weeks from decree to Messiah (the course’s scale test).
Scripture (KJV): 2 Peter 3:8–9 — “one day is with the Lord as a thousand years” is about the Lord’s patience, not a day-for-year rule.

little-horn.simple: A smaller horn rising among ten kings, “diverse” from them, that speaks against God, persecutes saints, and targets the sanctuary — read here as the papal church-state phase on Rome’s fragments.
little-horn.history: Daniel 7:24–25: the horn rises after the ten kings, subdues three kings, speaks great words against the Most High, wears out the saints, and reigns “until a time and times and the dividing of time” (3½ prophetic years → 1,260 year-days → A.D. 538–1798 in this chart). Daniel 8’s horn grows out of one of the four horns that replace Alexander’s great horn (8:8–9), toward the pleasant land, and takes away the daily sacrifice — pagan then papal Rome in succession. Antiochus IV is too early and too short for chapter 7’s checklist. Reformers applied the office to Rome; futurism relocated the same language to one end-time man.
proof: Scripture (KJV): Daniel 7:24–25 — diverse horn, three kings subdued, “a time and times and the dividing of time.”
Scripture (KJV): Daniel 8:9–13 — horn toward the pleasant land; the daily sacrifice taken away (8:11).
Primary: Newton 1733, Part I, Chap. VII — the eleventh horn and the Church of Rome (Gutenberg 16878).

chathak.simple: Hebrew chathak, rendered “determined” in the KJV of Daniel 9:24. The word occurs only there in the Hebrew Bible; its root means “cut,” and some historicist readers take the seventy weeks as cut from the longer 2,300-evening-morning span.
chathak.history: Daniel 8 ends with the 2,300 evening-mornings and the vision Daniel could not understand (8:14, 27). Daniel 9 opens with prayer; Gabriel returns with seventy weeks “determined upon thy people and upon thy holy city” (9:24). The course reads them as a first movement cut from the longer 2,300-evening-morning span, so that Messiah’s work can date the sanctuary question. Because the word occurs only once, weigh its meaning by context and root (“cut,” “decree”), not by parallel verses.
proof: Scripture (KJV): Daniel 9:24 — “Seventy weeks are determined upon thy people…” (Hebrew chathak).
Scripture (KJV): Daniel 8:14; 8:27 — the parent 2,300 span, left unexplained before chapter 9.
Lexical: chathak (Strong’s H2852) occurs once in the Hebrew Bible, at Daniel 9:24.

tamid.simple: Hebrew for the continual daily — the standing, regular priestly service before God, which Daniel 8 shows a horn attempting to replace with a counterfeit.
tamid.history: On earth the tamid was the regular sacrifice and ministry at the altar. In Daniel 8:11 the horn magnifies itself even to the Prince of the host; the daily sacrifice (the tamid) is taken away, and the place of his sanctuary is cast down — read in this course as an attack on Christ’s continual priesthood (Hebrews 7–10) through a competing earthly mediation. Sitting 10 links this to the papal phase; the chart’s 508 date is the course’s own reconstruction, not a number in Daniel 8.
proof: Scripture (KJV): Daniel 8:11–13 — the daily sacrifice taken away; the place of his sanctuary cast down.
Scripture (KJV): Hebrews 7:24–25 — Christ’s unchangeable priesthood as the New Testament counterpart.
Sittings 8–10 develop the sanctuary and tamid linkage.
Scripture (KJV): Daniel 1:1–2 — first siege in Jehoiakim’s third year; the Lord gave the king into Nebuchadnezzar’s hand.
Scripture (KJV): 2 Kings 23:36–24:6 — Jehoiakim’s reign; 2 Kings 24:1 — rebellion against Babylon; 24:6 — “So Jehoiakim slept with his fathers.”
Scripture (KJV): Jeremiah 25:1; 46:2 — the fourth year of Jehoiakim (Carchemish), set against Daniel 1:1’s third year (see Sitting 1).
Scripture (KJV): 2 Kings 24:8–16 — Jehoiachin carried away captive to Babylon; the second deportation.

Do not read BM 21946 as Daniel 1:1’s year; 605 and 597 stay separate.

Scripture (KJV): 2 Kings 25; Jeremiah 52 — third siege; the temple burned (586 B.C. in the course’s chart).

papacy.simple: The office of the bishop of Rome as a spiritual authority that, for long centuries, also wielded civil power over kings — the church-state reading of Daniel 7’s diverse little horn.
papacy.history: Daniel 7:24 says the horn shall be “diverse from the first” of the ten kings; the course reads that as religious plus political power, not merely pagan. This study applies that pattern to the historical papal office and its medieval–early modern supremacy, not to Roman Catholics as persons. Many Catholics sincerely follow Christ; the interpretation gives no warrant for prejudice. The chart’s dates: A.D. 538 (the Ostrogoths leave Rome) to 1798 (Berthier takes Pius VI captive). If 538 moves, 1798 moves on the same 1,260-year span.
proof: Scripture (KJV): Daniel 7:24–25 — diverse horn, saints worn out, “a time and times and the dividing of time.”
Primary: Newton 1733, Part I, Chap. VII — the eleventh horn and the Church of Rome (Gutenberg 16878).
History: Berthier’s entry into Rome and capture of Pius VI, 1798 (Sitting 7).
